paragraphs: Nectar robbing—the practice, common among certain bumblebees, of biting a hole in the base of a flower and extracting nectar without contacting its reproductive structures—has traditionally been classified as a straightforward case of exploitation. The robber obtains a reward while providing no pollination service, and the plant, deprived of nectar that would otherwise attract legitimate pollinators, presumably suffers reduced seed set. Field studies have confirmed this expectation for some species, but the effect is far from universal. In several populations of larkspur, for instance, robbed plants set as much seed as unrobbed ones, and in a few cases more.

One explanation for this unexpected result turns on the behavior of the legitimate pollinators themselves. A hummingbird that finds little nectar in the first few flowers of a plant tends to abandon that plant sooner and to fly farther before feeding again. Because many plants produce more viable seed when fertilized with pollen from distant, genetically dissimilar individuals than with pollen from near neighbors, this restlessness may partly offset the loss of visits. Robbing, in other words, may alter not merely how often a plant is pollinated but by whom—and with whose pollen.

Last year the Ferris County library system extended its weekday closing time from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. at every branch. In the twelve months that followed, the total number of items checked out from the system rose by 14 percent over the previous twelve months. Library administrators have concluded that the longer hours were responsible for the increase, and they now propose extending weekend hours as well.

Paleontologists have often taken the absence of tooth marks on fossilized bones from a site as evidence that predators did not scavenge the carcasses buried there. Modern crocodiles, however, swallow small prey whole and dismember large prey by twisting rather than chewing, and the bones of animals they have eaten frequently bear no marks at all. At sites where crocodilian fossils are abundant, therefore, unmarked bones are weak evidence that scavenging did not occur.

For much of the twentieth century, the debate over whether the early decades of British industrialization improved or worsened the lives of ordinary workers was conducted largely in the currency of wages. Optimists assembled series of money wages, deflated them by price indices, and found that real earnings rose, if slowly, from about 1820 onward; pessimists countered that the price indices omitted rents and other urban costs, that the wage series overrepresented skilled trades, and that averages concealed the long spells of unemployment that punctuated many working lives. Because each side could plausibly contest the other's data, the debate settled into a stalemate in which the choice of index seemed to determine the conclusion.

The introduction of anthropometric evidence in the 1980s promised a way out. Average adult height, which depends heavily on nutrition and exposure to disease during childhood and adolescence, offers a measure of well-being that is independent of prices altogether, and military recruitment records supplied measurements for hundreds of thousands of men born across the period. The results were striking: the average height of recruits appears to have declined for cohorts born in the second quarter of the nineteenth century, precisely when the optimists' wage series show real earnings improving. To many historians, the finding suggested that the gains captured by wages were offset by the crowding, polluted water, and epidemic disease that accompanied rapid urban growth.

Yet the height data have vulnerabilities of their own. Armies imposed minimum height requirements, and they lowered or raised those minimums as their need for men fluctuated; a sample of recruits is therefore truncated in ways that can manufacture apparent trends. Moreover, the men who volunteered for service were disproportionately drawn from those with poor civilian prospects, so that a decline in measured height might reflect a change in who enlisted rather than in the population at large. Statistical techniques have been devised to correct for truncation, but the correction for self-selection depends on assumptions about the civilian population that the records themselves cannot test. Anthropometric history has thus not so much resolved the old controversy as relocated it, from disputes about which prices belong in an index to disputes about who stood in line to be measured.

Planetary scientists commonly estimate the age of a planetary surface by counting the craters on it: the more densely cratered a surface, the longer it has presumably been exposed to impacts. The method's calibration rests on lunar rock samples whose ages have been determined radiometrically, which allow crater densities on the Moon to be converted into absolute ages. Applying that calibration to Mars or Mercury, however, requires assuming that the rate of impacts at those planets has borne a known relation to the rate at the Moon throughout their histories—an assumption that recent models of how the giant planets' orbits shifted early in the solar system's history have called into question. If those shifts sent waves of debris through the inner solar system at different times for different planets, then two surfaces with identical crater densities could differ considerably in age.

Two years ago a city transit agency installed real-time arrival displays at the stops along some of its bus routes. Since then, ridership on those routes has grown by 9 percent, compared with 2 percent on routes without displays. The agency's planners argue that installing displays along all remaining routes would raise ridership on those routes by a similar margin.
